prize_parts.citation: for the discovery of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos with the IceCube observatory, opening neutrino astronomy
for the development of optical lattice clocks based on the magic-wavelength principle, advancing precision measurement of time

statement.case_for: The two parts are both observational and instrument-led achievements that are well confirmed. IceCube observed the diffuse TeV-PeV astrophysical neutrino flux in a cubic-kilometre detector built in Antarctic ice. The result has been confirmed by several independent event samples and analyses, and corroborated by the TXS 0506+056 coincidence and the Galactic-plane neutrinos. It opened a new observational window, which is the strongest kind of claim I know how to test. Optical lattice clocks, from Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and first strontium clock to Ye's record stability and accuracy, reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18. They are reproduced in many national laboratories and are already used for relativistic geodesy, tests of fundamental constants and the coming redefinition of the second. Together the two parts are distinct in subject matter, give three laureates, and share the property that a new measurement capability produced a fresh view of nature. Neither depends on a still-contested interpretation.
statement.case_against: My opening ranked B016 first, but I accept it has the weakest support on the table, from only two members, and its attribution is the hardest part of my proposal. A single credited name for a collaboration-scale discovery, with AMANDA and the IceCube collaboration behind it, is a narrow reading of credit that the packet cannot settle. If the committee cannot identify a defensible set of individuals, the part should not carry the prize. For B013 the reservation is overlap with Hall and Hansch (2005, frequency combs) and Wineland (2012), and the pending redefinition of the second. Finally, the combination gives up the condensed-matter topic that most colleagues placed first, and a two-part prize is only justified if both halves are strong enough to stand alone.

responses.point: Ulf ranks IceCube first because it is a clear observation from nature, confirmed by later analyses including TXS 0506+056 and the Galactic plane, while accepting that one name cannot fairly represent a large collaboration.
responses.response: I agree on the observational strength and on timing. I would go further on the attribution problem than he did. Halzen as sole laureate is defensible only if outside experts confirm that the conceptual and organisational leadership was decisive, and I would not want to credit the discovery on a single name just to keep the prize small. I also think the source-identification gaps matter less than he suggests, because the prize would rest on the detection of the flux, not on its origin. Pairing B016 with a second, independent achievement is my way of not asking IceCube to carry the whole prize.

responses.point: Olle ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first because the flat-band prediction was followed by experimental discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity at the predicted angle, creating the moire field, with a theory-plus-experiment trio.
responses.response: This is the strongest rival to my configuration and I do not dismiss it, since five members placed it in their top three. My own rank of seven reflects my limited condensed-matter expertise, so I weigh his judgement heavily. My reservations are specific: the origin of the superconducting pairing is still debated, sample-to-sample variability is a known problem, and Andrei's independent early evidence makes the exclusion of one claimant real. I would ask whether the experimental credit between Jarillo-Herrero's group and Andrei's is cleanly separable. If colleagues can satisfy me on that, I would support B014 as a lead part, so I keep it as my first alternative.

responses.point: Eva Lindroth ranks optical lattice clocks first as an original, fundamental advance, with atoms held in light that does not disturb the counted transition, already used for geodesy and fundamental-constant tests. She calls the two-name allocation clean while noting other strontium and ytterbium groups.
responses.response: I agree with her on both the physics and the allocation, and she is better placed than I am to judge the atomic-physics detail. Where I differ from the reading some colleagues give is on the Hall-Hansch overlap: the comb was necessary but the lattice clock is a distinct concept with its own proof of performance, so I do not regard it as a double reward. I would, however, like her view on whether Ye's contribution is primarily the lattice clock or still shaded by the comb work, since that decides whether the pair is really Katori and Ye.

responses.point: Goran ranks circuit QED first, as a new regime of strong light-matter coupling in a solid-state circuit underpinning superconducting processors, while recognising that the 2025 prize already rewarded superconducting circuits and that allocation relative to Girvin and Devoret is delicate.
responses.response: I take his own timing caveat seriously and I think it is decisive for me. The 2025 prize already covered macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits, and the committee would risk appearing to reward the same ecosystem twice. Circuit QED is a real and distinct discovery, but with only two members ranking it and the credit unresolved against Girvin and Devoret, I cannot place it in my preferred configuration this year. I would be willing to revisit it if he can show why the 2025 recognition does not cover the strong-coupling regime.

uncertainties: Whether Halzen alone can credibly carry the IceCube credit, or whether the supplied packet omits decisive individuals.
Whether the committee would accept a two-part prize pairing astroparticle and precision-measurement work when most colleagues ranked condensed-matter topics first.
Whether the Hall-Hansch (2005) and Wineland (2012) prizes make optical lattice clocks look incremental before the redefinition of the second.
I cannot independently judge the condensed-matter allocations (B014, B041) and rely on colleagues and expert reviewers there.
statement.conflict_note: My profile shows I work in the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaborations and in astroparticle physics at KTH. IceCube is not among them, but it is a neighbouring field and I know people in that community, so I flag a possible recusal question on B016 for the committee to rule on. No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for the clocks or the condensed-matter candidates.
